posts.title: Why we only run four taps
posts.excerpt: A tight four-tap draught system keeps our cellar fresh, eliminates aged inventory, and serves every pint at peak quality.
posts.content:
A tight four-tap draught system keeps our cellar fresh, eliminates aged inventory, and serves every pint at peak quality.

When Ines Halvorsen and Tomas Achebe founded Awa Taproom in 2019, they faced a standard industry assumption: that a successful modern craft brewery needs dozens of draught handles line up along the back bar. Many taprooms boast twenty, thirty, or even fifty faucets pouring every conceivable style and experimental variation. From our small brick building at 214 Water Street in Bellingham, we chose an entirely opposite direction. Behind our long wooden bar, you will find exactly four stainless steel taps pouring cold beer into unbranded glasses. That single choice shapes everything we do, from our weekly brew schedule to the character of our hospitality.

The primary reason for running four taps is absolute cellar freshness. Beer is a living, delicate agricultural beverage that begins to deteriorate the moment it leaves the conditioning tank. In large multi-tap venues, kegs of niche or heavy beers often sit tapped in walk-in cold rooms for weeks or months, slowly losing their bright hop aromatics, crisp malt definition, and delicate carbonation. With four taps and thirty-eight seats—twelve at the bar and twenty-six across seven tables—our kegs turn over rapidly. Every beer on our draught board was brewed just weeks ago on our five-barrel brewhouse and transferred directly from one of our six fermenters.

This lean setup establishes an unbroken connection between our brewing schedule and the glasses in our guests' hands. Head brewer Ines Halvorsen and assistant brewer Priya Raman brew in five-barrel batches on Tuesday and Thursday mornings. The brew kettle and mash tun stand immediately behind the bar rail, meaning there are no supply chains, distribution trucks, or wholesale warehouses standing between our grain scoop and your seat. A beer finishes its three to five weeks of fermentation and cold conditioning, moves into Tomas Achebe's cellar kegs, and connects straight to the tap line. When a tap kicks, a new beer takes its place.

A four-tap board also demands intentional recipe design and balance across our four draught styles. On any given evening, our board offers a comprehensive spectrum of flavors without confusing clutter. Tonight, for example, we pour Foam Line Pale at 4.6% ABV with citrus peel notes, Tidewater Lager at 4.8% ABV with clean bread crust malt, Orchard Saison at 5.9% ABV with peppery dryness, and Night Shift Porter at 5.4% ABV with smooth cocoa depth. Pours are priced accessibly at $5 for 200 ml, $7 or $8 for 400 ml, and $14 for a tasting flight of all four. Every style serves a distinct purpose, leaving no dead weight on the line.

Finally, four taps cultivate a calm, unhurried atmosphere in the taproom. Rather than deciphering an overwhelming menu of sixty obscure options, guests can easily find a style that suits their mood and settle into conversation. Mireille Dufort and our bar team know every detail of each batch, from mash temperature to hop selection, because they walk past the boiling kettle every week. We believe that doing a few things with patience and precision creates a better neighborhood pub. We invite you to pull up one of our twelve bar stools, enjoy a fresh pour, and taste the difference that restraint makes.
